en: It was a place that would cause trouble.
For the weary soul, delight of life,
It is a place that will give refuge.
For those who flee in haste like us,
It is a place that will give shelter.
Pledging a hand to a saint,
Be a blessing, great poplar;
For orphans, widows and the destitute,
Be a father, great poplar.”
Setting Semetey at its foot,
Your poor mother, worn down,
Clasped the poplar tightly.
When she was truly at her wits’ end,
Kanykey let her words pour forth,
Beseeching that great poplar:
“If you are a saint, spread your hands;
Be a blessing, great poplar.
Parted from my saint,
We stand without shelter.
To poor people like us,
Be a father, great poplar!
We have despaired of our dear lives;
To find a little shelter,
Father, dear great poplar,
We have bowed before you!
I am exhausted: let me sleep my fill,
Dear great poplar.
I am weary: let my soul rest!
Let me sleep, great poplar;
Give strength to your orphan,
Beloved great poplar.
I have no provisions left: give me milk!
I am extinguished: kindle my fire.
Father great poplar, I am dead: revive my soul.
I have broken off: join me again.
Though you are lifeless, great poplar,
Ask after my condition!”
Thus, crying and wearing herself out,
For the sake of her orphan,
She beseeched the great poplar.
She turned her face toward the Truth;
Your noble sister-in-law Kanykey
Stood weeping openly.
(Much is false and much is true;
No one has come back having seen this.
Half is false and half is true;
No one has come from beside it.)
When she turned toward the Truth,
Your noble mother Kanykey,
Speaking and weeping,
Its leaves spread open.
The great poplar became a blessing;
For the wandering orphan and widows,
The great poplar became a father.
As the widow stood weeping,
Father great poplar began to hum.
As though there were a wind,
Swaying all by itself,
Father great poplar began to speak.
It had no tongue to speak like a human;
It cooed like a cuckoo.
From its root and crown,
Something spoke in a murmur.
Retreating from its foot,
Kanykey lost her strength.
On its north-facing side,
From the tip of one branch,
Milk flowed like a spring.
The hungry unfortunate ones
Held out their traveling bowls,
The milk that flowed pure white,
They caught and drank until soothed.
When they drank that milk,
Their painful places grew calm.
Kanykey and Chyyyrdy
Opened their eyes, wholly refreshed.
The fierce woman was stirred to walk;
When she drank that milk,
She regained her accustomed spirit.
Left in mourning, intent on fleeing,
Kanykey’s feet had grown raw.
For this sacred, unfortunate woman,
A great poplar, rather than a human, felt compassion.
At the great poplar’s foot, a broad shrine,
They lay down and slept their fill.
Resting on their sides, they soothed their souls;
Leaning on their elbows, they slept.
They dozed and took their rest,
Placing the orphan between them.
They put their thoughts out of mind,
Without opening their shut eyes,
Without drawing back their outstretched legs,
They lay and slept their fill.
Their hips grew utterly numb;
Thought after thought slipped away, unremembered.
The two ladies fell into deep sleep.
The two ladies began to snore.
Once the two ladies were asleep,
Forgetting the poor orphan,
Once they had fallen into deep sleep,
It was night, not daytime.
From his father back to his grandfather,
There was one who had always protected them.
Then the White Deer with twelve-branched antlers
Came running up
Your hero in the cradle,
Semetey, it saw.
Nudging his mouth and head,
With its hoof, the child’s
Swaddling it began to strike.
Circling the child three times,
It became his mother.
Slipping from his swaddling,
Semetey began to play.
He was then six months old,
At the age of crawling;
Semetey crawled away.
To the spur where the ridge ended,
To the headland of the plain,
Facing the qibla,
The orphan lay down on his side.
Protected thus by the White Holy Elder,
Semetey became a lord.
Offering its teat, the deer
Turned its neck aside.
Though called a stag, was it a hind?
To this child himself
It offered its teat.
When he sucked its teat, that hind
Felt it, do you see?
Facing the qibla,
At that moment the White Hind
Let down its milk, do you see?
Kanykey did not know;
Chyyyrdy had not noticed.
Waking with a start from sleep,
Your formidable mother Kanykey
Turned over to her right.
Reaching out her hand and looking,
Her only child was not in the swaddling.
What God has laid upon one’s head,
O warrior, there is no choice but to bear!
The banner fastened to her spear,
The gift left by the magnanimous one,
The child in the swaddling was gone.
Her heart could not hold so many thoughts.
Kanykey, born for grief,
Shed tears in ten streams.
Stunned and bereft of her senses,
Her comfort, the orphan Semetey—
Parted from her only one,
Then your fierce sister-in-law
Wept bitterly, unable to rise,
Crying and screaming, unable to find him:
“The prince’s only one,
Has his appointed death arrived as well?
My dark eyes clouded,
When I fell into deep sleep,
Did a dragon swallow him?
When I slept without tiring,
Did the giant bird, the Simurgh,
Lay its hand upon him?
Parted from my comfort,
O God, have I become like an extinguished fire?
My fortunate child is not in his swaddling;
Does death come to him in this way?
Parted from my only one,
Is this how a bitch is left helpless?
Because I have no perch,
My falcon has thus flown from my hand.
My beloved mother,
Because I have no glove,
My hero has slipped from my hand.
Where we might live grandly in delight,
There is no royal Kyrgyz city!
My beloved mother,
God has dug my pit;
He has set my misery boiling.
The child in this swaddling is gone!
My beloved mother,
When we fell asleep,
Your child in the swaddling—
Did a dragon swallow him?
This head that has known no good days,
Mother, has God cast it into grief?
Together our wings were broken;
We came out onto the plain for the child.
How shall we remain alive,
Parted from your only one, your orphan?
Instead of fleeing onward without a stop,
Mother, we turned aside and lodged, alas.
The lamp left by your son is gone;
Mother, we have become like an extinguished fire!
At this great poplar where we turned and lodged,
Mother, it was night, but not the Night of Power.
The only one left from my dear one is gone;
Now it is a day of cruel misfortune.
My dear, long thick hair,
Let me braid it down to my breast.
Parted from this only one,
Mother, let me die before my appointed death!”
Saying this to Chyyyrdy,
She took hold of a bright saber.
Toward the root of her heart
Kanykey brought it close.
Then the venerable lady Chyyyrdy,
The noblest of women,
Perhaps you have heard of her,
The mother of leopard Khan Manas—
She spread her arms.
“Do not stab yourself and take your life,” she said,
And seized the knife.
“Oh, Kanykey, my foal,
Do not act with such frenzy!
Crying out here between places,
My child, do not take your life so openly!
Do not settle along the river valley;
My child, do not die a needless death!
Upon your dear, doorlike teeth,
Let no wretched magpie shit.
If you stab yourself and die in torment,
Kanykey, my child, if I then die by mischance,
My foal, your Kyrgyz people are not here to bury us!
If these bones remain unburied,
My foal, if we lie sprawled upon the plain,
Our dear eyes, like blackcurrants,
Will a croaking vulture not gouge them out?
These sorrowful fugitives,
Will they not become crow shit?
With our backbone jutting bare,
Will the wretched vulture not tear it?
With our rib bones sticking out,
Will those accursed crows not shit upon them?
If we die needless deaths,
My child, will a wolf not gouge out our kidneys?
The tender flesh of our fat rumps,
Will foxes not sniff it and eat their fill?
‘They died through their own folly,’ they will say.
My child, would God’s servant not be shameless?
One of the seven days is death.
Kanykey, at last we shall die one day.
With both our cheeks blackened with soot,
When Judgment Day comes tomorrow,
My child, how shall we answer?
Kanykey, my child, do not cry;
Your support will be found alive.
My foal, my child, do not cry;
Do not wear away and torment your soul.
Pledged to Khojosan,
My foal Manas was a lion.
A servant of God Most High—
He will never create another like him again.
My foal Manas, my morning star,
His world was whole and complete;
He was a lion favored by the unseen patron.
His protector, Khojosan,
